events.title: Safari 5 released
events.summary: Apple released Safari 5 on June 7, 2010 at WWDC with Safari Reader, improved HTML5 support, and the Nitro JavaScript engine.
events.about: Safari 5 added Reader for distraction-free articles, extensions, and Bing as a search option. Nitro made JavaScript faster on Mac and Windows — keeping Safari relevant as Chrome gained share and developers tested HTML5 features.

narrative.whyChosen: Safari 5 bundled the HTML5 and Reader features that defined Apple's desktop browser era.
narrative.whyImportant: Extensions and Nitro JS kept WebKit competitive during the browser wars.
narrative.problemSolved: Safari 4 lacked extensions and felt behind Chrome's rapid feature releases.

events.title: iPhone 4 released
events.summary: Apple began selling the iPhone 4 on June 24, 2010 — with a Retina display, front-facing camera, and stainless-steel antenna band.
events.about: The Retina screen doubled pixel density to 326 ppi — designers and web developers started shipping @2x assets and `-webkit-device-pixel-ratio` media queries. FaceTime and the gyroscope expanded mobile app possibilities. The iPhone 4 cemented Apple's hardware lead and pushed mobile web design toward high-DPI layouts.

narrative.whyChosen: The iPhone 4's Retina display forced the mobile web and app ecosystems to adopt high-DPI assets.
narrative.whyImportant: It set the pixel-density bar every smartphone and responsive CSS workflow followed.
narrative.problemSolved: Mobile screens looked pixelated next to print; users expected sharper text and images on phones.

events.title: Samsung Galaxy S released
events.summary: Samsung began selling the Galaxy S in June 2010 — the first flagship Android phone in a line that would dominate smartphone sales.
events.about: The Galaxy S ran Android 2.1 with Samsung's TouchWiz skin and a 4-inch Super AMOLED display — establishing Samsung as Apple's primary Android hardware rival. Developers targeting Android tested on Galaxy devices as the default non-Nexus reference hardware for years.

narrative.whyChosen: The Galaxy S launched Samsung's flagship Android line that defined the iOS alternative.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved Android OEMs could ship premium hardware that competed with the iPhone at scale.
narrative.problemSolved: Android needed a flagship reference device beyond the G1 for mainstream consumers.
